titulo: Reported Speech, Backshift and Hedged Attribution
descripcion: Journalistic and careful professional English often reports what someone said while simultaneously distancing the writer from it: she reportedly claimed she had been unaware combines backshift, a reporting verb chosen for its connotation, and a hedge adverb, all in one clause.

filas: claim signals doubt, state is neutral
adds a further layer of distance

ejemplos.texto: She reportedly claimed she had been unaware of the decision.
He allegedly stated that the funds had already been transferred.
Officials reportedly admitted that the figures had been wrong.

notas: Claim carries an inbuilt note of doubt; state and say are neutral — choosing between them is itself a form of commentary.
Reportedly and allegedly both distance the writer from a claim, but allegedly specifically implies possible wrongdoing.
Overusing all three layers on every sentence makes a text read as needlessly suspicious rather than careful.

es.en: Spanish achieves a similar effect with según se dice or presuntamente, but rarely combines three distinct layers in one sentence as systematically as English journalism does. Spanish speakers tend to use one layer of distance where English expects two or three.
es.es: El español logra un efecto parecido con «según se dice» o «presuntamente», pero rara vez combina tres capas distintas en una sola oración de forma tan sistemática como el periodismo inglés. Los hispanohablantes tienden a usar una sola capa de distanciamiento donde el inglés espera dos o tres.

de.en: German marks distance with the Konjunktiv I, which does not change with the time of reporting, and with adverbs such as angeblich or Berichten zufolge. German speakers therefore often skip backshift (She said she is unaware) and rely on one adverb, where careful English combines backshift, a chosen reporting verb and a hedging adverb.
de.de: Deutsch markiert Distanz mit Konjunktiv I, der sich mit dem Zeitpunkt des Berichtens nicht verändert, und mit Adverbien wie «angeblich» oder «Berichten zufolge». Deutschsprachige lassen deshalb oft das backshift weg («She said she is unaware») und verlassen sich auf ein einzelnes Adverb, während sorgfältiges Englisch backshift, ein bewusst gewähltes reporting verb und ein hedging adverb kombiniert.

it.en: Italian journalism marks distance with the condizionale (avrebbe dichiarato di non sapere), which leads to the calque she would have claimed. Secondo quanto riportato corresponds well to reportedly; the English combination of backshift, reporting verb and adverb has to be learned as a pattern.
it.it: Il giornalismo italiano marca la distanza con il condizionale («avrebbe dichiarato di non sapere»), il che porta al calco «she would have claimed». «Secondo quanto riportato» corrisponde bene a «reportedly»; la combinazione inglese di backshift, reporting verb e avverbio va imparata come modello.

fr.en: The French conditionnel journalistique (elle aurait affirmé ne pas être au courant) leads to the calque she would have claimed. Selon and prétendument are useful, but prétendument is more sceptical than reportedly, so the choice of adverb needs care.
fr.fr: Le conditionnel journalistique français («elle aurait affirmé ne pas être au courant») conduit au calque «she would have claimed». «Selon» et «prétendument» sont utiles, mais «prétendument» est plus sceptique que «reportedly» ; le choix de l'adverbe demande donc de la précision.

pt.en: European Portuguese uses alegadamente very much like allegedly, and the press marks unconfirmed claims with the future perfect (terá afirmado), which leads to the calque she will have claimed. Backshift itself is familiar, as Portuguese reported speech shifts tenses in the same way.
pt.pt: O português europeu usa «alegadamente» de modo muito parecido com «allegedly», e a imprensa marca afirmações não confirmadas com o futuro perfeito («terá afirmado»), o que pode levar ao calque «she will have claimed». O backshift em si é familiar, pois o discurso indireto português também desloca os tempos.

errores: Choosing claim where a neutral verb like state or say would be more accurate and fair.
Stacking all three layers on a fact that is actually verified, which reads as unfairly doubtful.
Getting the backshift wrong when combining it with a reporting verb of doubt.

autochequeo: Does the reporting verb (claim, state, say) match the actual level of certainty?
Is the distancing adverb (reportedly, allegedly) appropriate to the situation?
Have I avoided stacking all three layers on a verified fact?
Would a reader sense fairness rather than unwarranted suspicion?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on reported speech combined with hedged attribution. Check the reporting verb choice, the backshift and whether the distancing feels fair to the source. Do not rewrite the text.

es: Copying the reportive conditional («*según el informe, los costes habrían subido*»): *costs would have risen* instead of *costs have reportedly risen*.
de: Keeping the present after a past reporting verb, as with «Konjunktiv I» («*er sagte, er sei krank*»): *He said he is ill* where the backshift is expected.
it: Copying the reportive conditional («*secondo il rapporto, i costi sarebbero aumentati*»): *costs would have risen* instead of *costs have reportedly risen*.
fr: Copying the reportive conditional («*selon le rapport, les coûts auraient augmenté*»): *costs would have risen* instead of *costs have reportedly risen*.
pt: Copying the reportive conditional («*segundo o relatório, os custos teriam subido*»): *costs would have risen* instead of *costs have reportedly risen*.
